facts.text: On this date in 1962, Jamaica's first prime minister led the country into independence — yet Jamaica still holds the record for most Olympic medals won per capita by a Caribbean nation, driven almost entirely by track and field.
On this date in 1582, October 5th simply did not exist in Catholic Europe. Pope Gregory XIII's calendar reform skipped ten days overnight, jumping straight from October 4th to October 15th.

The most densely populated place on Earth is not a city — it is Dhaka's Korail slum, where over 100,000 people share a single square kilometer, outnumbering Manhattan at its most crowded by a factor of four.

Monaco has more millionaires per capita than any nation on Earth, yet it fields a full-time military of 82 soldiers — roughly one soldier for every 50 residents of its single high-rise-dense square mile.
Indonesia spans a wider longitude than the continental United States, yet it contains over 700 living languages, more than the entire African continent's linguistic diversity per square kilometer.
On this day in 1987, the Dow fell 91 points — its worst single-day drop in two years. Eleven days later, Black Monday erased 22% in a single session, the largest one-day crash in Wall Street history.
On this day in 1929, the London Stock Exchange collapsed weeks before Wall Street followed. The British crack came first, triggered by the arrest of financier Clarence Hatry for fraud.
The S&P 500 has closed higher on the day after a U.S. presidential election roughly 80% of the time, regardless of which party won.
Berkshire Hathaway was originally a textile company. Warren Buffett later called buying it the worst trade of his life — a $200 billion mistake born from spite over a lowball tender offer.
The Dutch East India Company, history's first publicly traded firm, was so large at its peak that its inflation-adjusted value exceeds the combined market cap of today's five largest companies.
On this date in 1923, Edwin Hubble identified a Cepheid variable star in Andromeda, proving our galaxy is not the universe — just one of billions.
On October 5, 1984, Marc Garneau became Canada's first astronaut in space, aboard a shuttle carrying a payload that included shrimp development experiments.
Your skeleton is not static scaffolding. Every decade, your body replaces nearly all of its bone mass through a process called remodeling, run by cells that eat and rebuild you continuously.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A single teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of photoreceptors — four times more than humans — yet process color worse. More channels, it turns out, does not mean richer perception.
On this day in 1962, the Beatles released their debut single 'Love Me Do' — the same year Walmart opened its first store. Two icons, one autumn.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. It held lectures before Tenochtitlán had a single stone laid.
On this day in 1930, the R101 airship crashed in France, killing 48, and effectively ended Britain's imperial airship program overnight.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The ancient world had its own ancient history.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, before electric lighting reached a single home.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Already feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home you cannot return to — or that never existed. No single English word comes close, which says something about what English chooses not to carry.
On this day in 1582, October 5 did not exist in Catholic countries. The Gregorian calendar reform skipped ten days, and people went to sleep on October 4 and woke up on October 15.
Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of used bookshops, also from Koenig's invented lexicon. That it needed inventing — and immediately felt familiar — is the real fact here.
On October 5, 1962, the word 'Beatles' entered the cultural record permanently when Love Me Do was released. The name fuses 'beat' and 'beetles,' a pun that took over the planet.

On this date in 2021, the SEC rejected VanEck's Bitcoin ETF application — the 8th such rejection in four years. Spot Bitcoin ETFs finally launched in the US in January 2024, 11 years after the first application.
On this date in 2008, Satoshi Nakamoto sent the Bitcoin whitepaper to the cryptography mailing list for the first time — a 9-page PDF that created a $1T+ asset class.
Bitcoin's UTXO model means your wallet balance doesn't exist on-chain. What exists are discrete unspent outputs, each with its own locking script — closer to physical coins than a bank ledger.
The DAO hack in 2016 drained 3.6M ETH via a reentrancy bug. The attacker couldn't move the funds immediately due to a 28-day lock — giving Ethereum enough time to hard fork and reverse the theft.

Ethereum validators must wait in an exit queue to withdraw staked ETH. At peak congestion in 2023, that queue stretched to over 40 days — a deliberate throttle to prevent mass destabilization of the consensus layer.

On this date in 2011, Apple launched Siri — the first mainstream neural-network voice assistant. It was widely mocked as unreliable. Fourteen years later, its core architecture looks quaint beside the models it helped normalize.
On this date in 2015, the first version of TensorFlow was open-sourced by Google Brain. Within 18 months it had more GitHub stars than any machine learning project in history.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average U.S. homes, spent in a matter of months.

AlphaFold 2 predicted the structures of over 200 million proteins before most structural biology labs had time to read the original paper. It effectively compressed decades of wet-lab work into a single release.

The first computer program to beat a world champion at a board game was not a neural network. IBM's Deep Blue defeated Kasparov in 1997 using handcrafted evaluation functions and brute-force search — no learning involved.
